newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan MITI chief calls for lower electricity rates.
newsitem.headline: Japan MITI chief calls for lower electricity rates.

text.p: Japan's trade minister reiterated the need to cut the nation's electricity rates to levels comparable with those overseas in a meeting with leading power utility companies on Thursday.

Trade Minister Shinji Sato was quoted by a ministry official as saying that one of the government's priorities was to ease regulations relating to industries that were not cost-conscious in order to make them so.
Sato said this included power utilities.
"The most important issue is to correct the nature of Japan's electricity industry, which is not cost-conscious," he was quoted as saying.
The official of the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI) briefing reporters quoted Sato as saying that lowering electricity rates was a goal.
Sato reportedly said: "Japan has set a target of reducing electricity rates to levels comparable to those overseas by 2001 in its economic programme (issued last year)."
"I would like the energy industry to do everything within its power to try to achieve this aim," he said.
The comments were made at a breakfast meeting between Sato and the heads of the power utility industries.

Despite pressure to cut electricity rates, Japan's leading public utilities said last month they will raise electricity rates this spring, citing climbing fuel costs and a scheduled rise in the consumption tax to five percent from three percent in April.
Japan's utility industry reviews its rates every quarter, taking into account the cost of fuel.
Based on last September's foreign exchange rates, the electricity fee paid by the average Japanese home was roughly 30 percent higher than in the United States and 20 percent higher than in Germany.

Japan's wholesale electricity business was liberalised following a revision in a utility industry law in December 1995, paving the way for non-utilities to sell electricity on a wholesale basis to power companies.
